latin.707: Veniamus ad vers. 14. Sed regnavit mors etiam in eos qui non peccaverunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adae, qui est typus futuri. Hic tu recte observas Apostolum causam inferre ex effectu, ac probare, omnes peccasse, quia mors regnavit in omnes; ac sic formas argumentum Apostoli, debuisti dicere, tuum. Apostoli enim longe abest a mente.
latin.708: Ubi mors regnat, nec est reatus ex peccato proprio actuali, ibi necessario est imputatio reatus primi peccati. At ante legem mors regnavit, etiam in eos in quibus non fuit reatus ex peccato proprio, nempe in parvulos. Ergo infantibus reatus primi peccati necessario fuit imputatus.
latin.709: Tu ipse vidisti negari posse maiorem: nam praeter reatum ex proprio peccato actuali, & quem frustra probare conaris ex peccato actuali Adae imputato, est reatus ex proprio peccato innato, & ut ita loquar, habituali.
latin.710: Itaque obviam is, Nec cavillandum est, inquis, reatum in illis esse a vitio inhaerente, & a prava dispositione & corruptione. Nam unde fit, ut rei & corrupti nascantur, nisi quod in Adamo inclusi in illo peccarunt, ut dixit Apostolus, & peccatum illius ipsis imputatum fuit, ut sint rei corrupti? Nondum enim voluntate propria peccarunt, nec cogitatione, nec verbis, nec actione. Inde sic concludo, Quicunque moriuntur sunt peccatores. Pueri in utero matrum, aut recens nati moriuntur, ut constat experientia. Ergo pueri in utero matrum & recens nati sunt peccatores. Si sunt peccatores, ideo sunt, vel quod actu peccaverint, vel quod primum peccatum primi parentis ipsis imputetur. Tertium siquidem dari non potest, quod illos constituat peccatores. Nam peccator quis dicitur ob peccatum; nec ullum aliud peccatum potest imputari, nisi illud primum.
latin.711: Quid est negare vitii inhaerentis seu corruptionis innatae reatum, si hoc non est? Putarem tibi ista excidisse imprudenti aestu disputationis abrepto in Pighiani erroris scopulum, nisi te viderem diu haerentem & versantem in hac re probanda, & inculcanda: quod a te factum esse, pro eo quo te prosequor amore, vehementer doleo. Dubium autem mihi non est quin admonitus statim pedem ex hoc errore referas, quem tu ipse Cap. 2. huius tui tractatus refutasti, aut saltem refutare prae te tulisti. Ego certe multo pluribus refutarem si mihi aut cum Pelagio, aut cum Pighio, aut cum Pontificio aliquo (quanquam Pontificii hoc vitium inhaerens ante baptismum peccatum esse confitentur, sed post baptismum negant) negotium esset. Nunc cum sit mihi res tecum, fratre, synamista, religionem reformatam profitente & docente; te vel semel monuisse satis esse puto.
latin.712: Pauca tamen quaedam respondebo tibi. Quaeris unde fit ut peccatores & corrupti nascantur? Respondeo nos eos peccatores esse, quoniam corrupti nascimur; nullum enim in infante, cum nascitur, reatum agnosco, cuius fundamentum & causa non sit corruptio inhaerens. Si rursus quaeras unde fiat, ut nascantur corrupti? Respondebo quia nascimur ex corrupto parente. Sic quaerenti, cur homo natus sim? Respondeo, quia natus sum ex homine; cur vitiosus? Quia natus sum ex vitioso. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est. De naturae peccato vitio: non nisi natura nascitur vitiosi, id est, peccatrix, secundum quod ait Apostolus Paulus, Qualis terrenus, tales & terreni; & hoc quomodo nisi per seminis transfusionem? Sed his ipsis quaestionibus iam supra pluribus satisfeci. Haec corruptio, quae & concupiscentia, & peccatum antonomastice, & peccatum peccans dici solet, quaeque in irregenitis regnat, in regenitis habitat, primum est peccatum nostrum, scaturigo ceterorum. Ab ea primus noster reatus nascitur, imputata nobis ad mortem. Moriuntur ergo infantes non ob peccatum alienum, videlicet actuale Adami sibi imputatum, sed ob proprium inhaerens, insitum. At, inquis, Infantes nondum voluntate propria peccarunt, nec cogitatione, nec verbis, nec actione. Ergo non habent proprium peccatum: actuale quidem concedo, habituale vero pernego. Distingue igitur, si placet, inter peccatum quod est actio vel omissio actionis, & peccatum quod est ad eiusmodi actionem vel omissionem propensio, proclivitas, habitus.

pass_a.707: Placeus turns to Rom. 5:14 (death reigned even over those who did not sin after Adam’s likeness; Adam a type of the Coming One). Garissoles rightly notices cause-from-effect—all sinned because death reigned over all—but the syllogism he frames is his own, not the Apostle’s mind.
pass_a.708: Placeus restates the form Garissoles needs: where death reigns and there is no reatus from one’s own actual sin, Adam’s first-sin reatus must be imputed; before the law death reigned even over parvuli without own-sin reatus; therefore infants had Adam’s reatus necessarily imputed.
pass_a.709: Placeus: you already saw the major can fall. Besides own actual reatus and the Adam-act imputation you labor to prove, there is reatus from own innate—habitual—sin.
pass_a.710: Garissoles meets the innate-vice reply: do not cavil that infants’ reatus is from inherent corruption; they are born guilty only because enclosed in Adam they sinned in him and his sin was imputed. They have not yet willed, thought, spoken, or acted sin. Whoever die are sinners; womb-children and newborns die; so they are sinners—either by own act or by first-parent sin imputed; no third way constitutes them sinners; a sinner is named for sin, and only that first sin can be imputed to them.
pass_a.711: Placeus: denying the reatus of inherent vice or innate corruption—if Garissoles’s chain is not that denial, what is? He would excuse a slip in the heat of dispute onto Pighius’s reef, but sees Garissoles long stuck proving and pressing the point, and for brotherly love deeply regrets it. He trusts one warning will pull the foot back from an error Cap. 2 already claimed to refute. Against Pelagius, Pighius, or a Papist he would multiply arguments (Papists grant inherent vice as sin before baptism, deny it after); with a Reformed brother and fellow-teacher, one admonition is enough.
pass_a.712: Placeus answers briefly the unde question. We are called sinners because we are born corrupt: in a newborn he acknowledges no reatus whose ground and cause is not inherent corruption. Ask again why we are born corrupt, and the reply is generation from a corrupt parent—human from human, vicious from vicious; what is born of flesh is flesh. Nature’s sinful vice propagates only by nature: as Paul says, as was the earthly man, so are the earthly, by transfusion of seed—questions already answered at length above. This corruption, also named concupiscence, sin by antonomasia, and sinning sin, reigns in the unregenerate and dwells in the regenerate; it is our first sin and the spring of the rest, and from it our first reatus arises, imputed unto death. Infants therefore die not for Adam’s alien actual sin imputed, but for their own inherent, implanted sin. To the objection that they have not yet sinned by will, thought, word, or deed: no own actual sin—granted; no habitual?—flatly denied. Distinguish sin as act or omission from sin as propensity, proclivity, and habit toward such act or omission.

707: Let us come to verse 14: But death reigned even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come.
Here you rightly observe that the Apostle infers a cause from an effect, and proves that all have sinned because death reigned over all;
and so you form the Apostle’s argument—you ought to have said, your own.
For it is far from the Apostle’s mind.
708: Where death reigns, and there is no reatus from one’s own actual sin, there the imputation of the reatus of the first sin is necessary.
But before the law death reigned, even over those in whom there was no reatus from their own sin—namely, over little ones.
Therefore the reatus of the first sin was necessarily imputed to infants.
709: You yourself have seen that the major can be denied: for besides the reatus from one’s own actual sin, and the one you try in vain to prove from Adam’s actual sin imputed, there is a reatus from one’s own innate sin—and, so to speak, habitual.
710: And so you meet it: It must not be cavilled, you say, that the reatus in them is from inherent vice, and from a depraved disposition and corruption.

For whence comes it that they are born guilty and corrupt, unless that, enclosed in Adam, they sinned in him, as the Apostle said, and his sin was imputed to them, so that they are guilty and corrupt?
For they have not yet sinned by their own will, nor by thought, nor by words, nor by deed.
From this I conclude thus: Whoever die are sinners.
Children in their mothers’ wombs, or newly born, die, as experience shows.
Therefore children in the womb and the newly born are sinners.
If they are sinners, they are so either because they have sinned in act, or because the first sin of the first parent is imputed to them.
For a third cannot be given that would constitute them sinners.
For one is called a sinner because of sin; and no other sin can be imputed except that first one.
711: What is it to deny the reatus of inherent vice or innate corruption, if this is not it?

I would think these things had slipped from you, carried off by the imprudent heat of dispute onto the reef of Pighius’s error, did I not see you long stuck and turning in proving and pressing this very point—which, for the love with which I pursue you, I deeply regret has been done by you.

Yet I have no doubt that, once warned, you will at once draw your foot back from this error, which you yourself in Cap. 2 of this treatise of yours have refuted, or at least put yourself forward as refuting.

I certainly would refute it with far more, if I had business with Pelagius, or with Pighius, or with some Papist (though the Papists confess this inherent vice to be sin before baptism, but deny it after baptism).
Now, since my matter is with you—brother, fellow-worker, professing and teaching the Reformed religion—I judge it enough to have warned you even once.
712: Yet I will answer you a few things.
You ask whence it comes that we are born sinners and corrupt?
I answer that we are sinners because we are born corrupt; for in an infant, when he is born, I acknowledge no reatus whose foundation and cause is not inherent corruption.
If again you ask whence it comes that they are born corrupt? I will answer: because we are born of a corrupt parent.
So to one asking, Why was I born a human? I answer, Because I was born of a human; why vicious? Because I was born of a vicious one.
What is born of flesh is flesh.

Of the vice of nature’s sin: the vicious—that is, the sinner—is born only by nature, according to what the Apostle Paul says, As was the earthly man, so also are the earthly; and how, unless by transfusion of seed?
But to these very questions I have already satisfied at length above.

This corruption—which is also commonly called concupiscence, and sin by antonomasia, and sinning sin, and which reigns in the unregenerate and dwells in the regenerate—is our first sin, the spring of the rest.
From it our first reatus is born, imputed to us unto death.
Infants therefore die not for an alien sin—namely Adam’s actual sin imputed to them—but for their own inherent, implanted sin.
But, you say, Infants have not yet sinned by their own will, nor by thought, nor by words, nor by deed.
Therefore they have no own sin: the actual, I grant; the habitual, I flatly deny.
Distinguish, then, if you please, between sin that is an act or an omission of an act, and sin that is a propensity, proclivity, habit toward such an act or omission.
